notes.meaning: David prays that God will give his royal son the wisdom to govern well. An earthly king needed God's own standard of right and wrong to lead the nation fairly. Christian readers also see this as a picture of Jesus, the true Son of David who receives all authority and judgment from God the Father.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explained that God the Father gives all judgment to God the Son, who is both the King and the King's Son because the Father is also King.

notes.meaning: The king is called to govern all citizens with fairness and show special care to the weak. In Israel, true justice meant defending those who could not protect themselves. This kind of fair rule reflects the gentle, righteous leadership of Christ over his people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine views God's people and the afflicted as the same group, teaching that all of God's people are called to be humble and poor in spirit.

notes.meaning: The hills and mountains picture the whole land sharing in peace and fruitfulness under good government. In ancient times, hills were often dangerous places where robbers hid. Under a just king, travel becomes safe and even rugged ground produces rich crops.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that the mountains and hills stand for great leaders and ordinary believers in the church who are called to live together in peace.

notes.meaning: A good ruler uses his power to rescue helpless families from bullies and cheats. God gives kings authority precisely to protect the innocent and punish cruel oppressors. Ultimately, Christ breaks the power of all who harm his people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine viewed the oppressor here primarily as the devil, whom Christ overcomes to set his people free.

notes.meaning: The people will revere God and honor his king as long as the sun and moon shine. While Solomon's reign brought temporary awe, lasting reverence across every generation belongs only to God and the unending kingdom of Christ.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explains that the sun represents Christ's body on earth, the Church, which will continue through all generations.

notes.meaning: The king's gentle rule refreshes the land just like spring rain watering a cut field. Instead of acting like a harsh tyrant, a godly ruler brings life and relief to his subjects. In the same way, Christ revives thirsty hearts through the work of his Spirit and his word.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine reads the Hebrew word as fleece rather than grass, seeing Gideon's dew-covered fleece as a symbol of grace given through Christ.

notes.meaning: Good people thrive under a righteous leader, and lasting peace spreads throughout the land. Solomon gave Israel years of peace, but this verse looks forward to an eternal peace that never runs out. It points to Christ, who gives deep and endless peace to those who trust him.

This prayer asks for the king's rule to stretch from the sea to the Euphrates River, and across the whole world. Solomon ruled a wide region, but these words look beyond earthly borders to the worldwide reign of Jesus. His kingdom gathers people from every corner of the earth.

Even distant, wandering desert tribes will bow down to this king in deep respect. To lick the dust describes the ancient custom of bowing face-down to the ground before a monarch. All enemies will eventually surrender to his rightful rule.

Rulers from rich coastal lands in the west and wealthy nations in the south bring gifts to honor the king. This happened in part when the Queen of Sheba visited Solomon with treasures. It also points forward to distant lands honoring Christ with their finest offerings.

Every earthly ruler and foreign nation will bow before this king and serve him. Solomon received honor from nearby rulers, but no ordinary king ever ruled every nation on earth. This universal worship will be given fully only to Jesus.

The king wins world renown not by brutal conquest, but by showing mercy to the helpless. When poor people who have no human helper cry out, he listens and saves them. Jesus leads in this same way by rescuing anyone who admits their weakness and asks for help.

A good ruler feels deep pity for the weak and saves them from death. Instead of crushing the needy to make himself rich, he protects their very lives like a caring father. Christ shows this tender mercy by guarding both the bodies and the souls of his people.

The king rescues his people from dirty schemes and violent attacks. To say their blood is precious means he treats their lives as extremely valuable, never letting them be wasted or harmed without justice. Christ acts as our redeemer, paying the highest price to set us free from danger.

The people wish their king a long and healthy life, offering him fine gold and continuous prayers. Subjects joyfully pray for God to bless their ruler because his reign brings them safety and joy. In Christ's kingdom, believers constantly praise his name and pray for his kingdom to advance.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators suggest that the person who lives and gives gold is the rescued poor man from the previous verse, who now prays for and blesses his royal protector.

notes.meaning: The land will be packed with grain, even waving like a dense forest high up on the mountain ridges. Under God's blessing, crops overflow and city populations multiply like lush grass in a field. Material prosperity in the psalm pictures the rich spiritual blessings found in the kingdom of God.

The king's fame will continue through every generation, outlasting the sun. God's ancient promise to Abraham—that all families of the earth would be blessed through him—is fulfilled through this royal line. Jesus is the ultimate King in whom all nations find true and everlasting blessing.

The writer closes with high praise to the LORD God of Israel, the only one who does miraculous deeds. He prays that God's glorious presence and honor will spread across the entire globe. Saying amen twice shows strong agreement and joyful certainty that this will happen.

This closing note marks the end of Book Two of the Psalms, which gathered many of David's prayers. Having prayed for the future king and seen God's great plan, David's deepest hopes for his family and kingdom were answered. Other psalms of David appear later in the Bible, but this special collection here reaches its finish.
